does: Toasts sesame seeds until they are fragrant, then grinds them in a ridged bowl to a rough, oily paste with some seeds left half whole, ready to coat vegetables or to thicken a dressing.

intro.what: This method toasts sesame and grinds it into a rough, oily paste for dressings and vegetables.
intro.why: It shows how to develop a nutty scent while retaining some seed texture instead of making a greasy paste.

how: Toast the seeds in a dry pan, shaking them, until they smell nutty and begin to pop.
Tip them into the ridged bowl while they are still warm.
Grind them with a circular motion, pressing against the ridges, until they are half crushed and oily.
Stir in the other seasonings and use the paste right away, as its scent fades.

cues.text: A deep, nutty, warm scent rises from the bowl.
The mixture turns into a damp, oily paste with some seeds left whole.

mistakes.mistake: Grinding raw seeds, which gives a pale, flat taste.
Grinding too long, which turns the paste greasy and pasty.
mistakes.fix: Stop while the seeds are still half whole.

quiz.question: Why toast sesame before grinding it here?
choices: To keep the seeds pale and raw-tasting.
To develop a nutty scent and fuller taste.
To dry out all the oil in the seeds.
quiz.because: Toasting brings out the nutty scent missing from raw ground seeds.

quiz.question: How do you work the seeds in the ridged bowl?
choices: Tap lightly without pressing against the ridges.
Wait until cold and stir without crushing.
Press and grind in circles while they are still warm.
quiz.because: Pressing against the ridges breaks the toasted seeds into a rough paste.

quiz.question: Which texture should remain in the ground sesame?
choices: A damp, oily paste with some seeds still partly whole.
Loose dry seeds without any crushed paste.
quiz.because: This method stops with a rough texture and some visible seeds, rather than grinding everything smooth.

quiz.question: The paste has become greasy and pasty. What would you change next time?
choices: Grind longer to absorb the oil.
Stop grinding while some seeds remain partly whole.
Skip toasting and grind until smooth.
quiz.because: Overgrinding loses the intended rough seed texture and makes the paste greasy.

variant_of.differs: The seeds are ground only until half crushed, in a ridged bowl, so that the paste stays rough and oily instead of becoming fine powder.
